To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

replication of CMV, EBV and KSVH persists in many HIV-infected patients who receive suppressive antiretoviral therapy but that such herpesvirus replication, measured in saliva specimens, does not appear to be associated with the degree of CD8+ T cells expressing activation markers or with the failure to achieve absolute CD4+ cell counts above 500/µL in the face of suppressive antiretorviral therapy.

replication of CMV and other human herpesviruses persists in many antiviral-suppressed, immunocompromised HIV-infected patients but is not associated with abnormally elevated CD8+ T cells and subnormal CD4+ T cells counts.

we did not find evidence in this case-control study that ongoing CMV, EB Virus and Kaposi sarcoma virus replication in saliva is associated with higher T cell activation and low CD4+ T cells in patients receiving suppressive antiretoviral therapy.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of CMV, KSHV and EBV in the pathogenesis of HIV disease.
HIV-1 infection and the development of AIDS.

the mechanisms that underlie the persistence of immune activation and inflammation in patients receiving suppressive antiretoviral therapy, and we have not found evidence to implicate the degree of human herpesvirus reactivation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the degree of ongoing CMV, EB and KSHV replication is not associated with the magnitude of generalized T cell activation and low CD4+ T counts in HIV-infected patients with effective antiretroviralt therapy.
the presence of CMV, KSHV or EBV DNA in saliva does not appear to be an independent predictor of abnormal T cell activation in HIV-infected patients.

the magnitude of CMV, KSHV and EBV replication is not associated with abnormally elevated CD8+ T cells CD38+HLADR+ expression and sub-optimal CD4+ T cells counts in the face virologically-suppressive antiretrovirus therapy in HIV-infected patients.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the presence of human herpesvirus DNA in saliva is common in antiretrovially suppressed HIV-infected patients and the degree of human herpesviral replication is not associated with abnormal T cell activation and failure to achieve normal CD4+ T cells counts.

the degree of human herpesvirus reactivation in saliva is low in antiretrovirus-suppressed HIV-infected persons, but that the magnitude of reactivation is not associated with abnormal CD8+ T lymphocyte activation or sub-normal absolute CD4+ cell counts.
the degree of human herpesvirus (CMV, EBV, and KSHV) replication is not associated with abnormal CD8+ T-cell activation or subnormal CD4+ T-cell count recovery after long-term suppressive ART.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we have developed a new assay for the detection and quantitation of CMV,EBV and KSHVS DNA in saliva.
the presence of herpesviruses in saliva is not associated with abnormal T cell activation and low CD4 counts in patients on antiretrovial therapy.
the presence of human herpesvirus DNA in saliva is not associated with abnormal T cell activation and low CD4+ T cells counts in patients receiving suppressive antiretoviral therapy.
